source_read: PMC HTML (PMC2561112), full text read in my own browser tab on 2026-11-01: abstract, search strategy, all sections, Table 1, figure captions (Figures 1-2 plot Table 1 values with the printed r; Figures 3-5 are conceptual diagrams without data), conclusion and reference list

claims.overstatement: None; the claim labels the review's figures second-hand. 'Wide and overlap' is fair for the quoted lethal ranges (the published methadone ranges overlap one another, and the author states that opioids show little or no separation between therapeutic and toxic concentrations); the review has no data of its own on overlap with deaths from other causes. The tolerance point (opioid amounts lethal to unexposed people are survived by people who use heroin habitually) is the author's general statement without a cited study.
claims.note: Narrative review by one clinical pharmacologist with a stated EMBASE/Medline search to June 2007 plus a personal collection; no selection rules or appraisal. The MDMA and methadone ranges come from ref. 38 (Gable, 2004). Reporting slips: the ethanol '95% confidence interval' (185-526 mg/100 mL) is a range of individual values from the SD, not a CI of the mean; the median arm-leg methadone difference is printed in µmol/L (72, IQR 20-200), which cannot fit the µg/L ranges beside it.

anchors.locator: Quantitative post-mortem analysis › Extrapolation from post-mortem concentrations to ante-mortem concentrations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Quoted lethal concentration ranges in modern data (ref. 38): MDMA 40-8500 µg/L, methadone 60-3100 µg/L. Milroy & Forrest (ref. 39) found lethal methadone concentrations quoted variously as 220-3040, 200-4500, 320-3980, 1000-2000, and 100-2500 (intravenous) or 100-2600 µg/L (oral); their own 111 deaths ranged 84-2700 µg/L; in 25 with arm and leg blood the median difference was 72 (IQR 20-200), units printed as µmol/L.

anchors.locator: Quantitative post-mortem analysis › Importance of tolerance, 1st-2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: For opioids and many cancer drugs there is little or no separation between therapeutic and toxic concentrations; repeated exposure (opioids, GABA agonists including ethanol) shifts concentration-response curves. Ethanol: a patient still talking at >1500 mg/100 mL, three times a quoted fatal value; 693 deaths from acute alcohol poisoning (Jones & Holmgren) averaged 356 mg/100 mL, 95% of values about 185-526, so lethal levels differed threefold. More than one drug is commonly implicated, adding interactions.

anchors.locator: Making deduction from post-mortem drug concentrations, 3rd paragraph (after Figures 3-4); Figure 5 caption
anchors.extracted: Even if deaths could be sorted into drug-induced and not drug-induced, concentrations in the two groups would very likely overlap (biological, sampling and analytical variability); opioid doses lethal to unexposed people are tolerated by people who use heroin habitually; Figure 5 is a hypothetical illustration with no data.

anchors.locator: Making deduction from post-mortem drug concentrations, 2nd paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: A reliable lethal concentration needs a series of deaths with the drug detected, each assigned to drug-induced or not without knowledge of the measured concentration, then a comparison of the two groups; such assignment is difficult (unobserved deaths, hidden causes such as arrhythmia); the author expects broad overlap and judges that post-mortem concentrations have been over-interpreted.

anchors.locator: Qualitative post-mortem analysis, 2nd paragraph; False-positive results, 1st-3rd paragraphs; False-negative results, 1st-2nd and 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: A positive test for a poison does not by itself establish that it caused death, nor a negative test that it did not. False positives: non-specific assays, substances formed after death (ethanol, GHB) or contamination; false negatives: substances not specifically tested for, or drug gone before death (paracetamol, paraquat). Both kinds occur.

Comparing a case's concentration with earlier cases attributed to poisoning is potentially misleading without knowing post-mortem changes and without comparison material from people taking the drug who died of other causes.

claims.overstatement: None; 'thought least open to change' matches the source's hedged wording, and the whole-blood/plasma point is stated as in the source.
claims.note: The claim cites the review only for two narrow points; the review also supports the headline (site- and time-dependent change in both directions, not predictable from volume of distribution or lipid solubility), with second-hand human ratios. Table 1 reproduces Leikin & Watson's central-to-peripheral ratios (e.g. morphine 2.2), and the review notes they carry no stated uncertainty. Ferner's ref. 68 (Elliott & Burgess, 2005, urinalysis in suspected drink-spiking) does not match the MDMA ante/post-mortem ratios it is cited for.

anchors.extracted: Almost all post-mortem analysis is on whole blood, whereas assays in living patients are mostly on plasma or serum; femoral venous blood is thought to be least susceptible to post-mortem change; failing that, heart or other central blood is used; for many drugs peripheral and central post-mortem concentrations differ markedly (Table 1).

Even in life the whole-blood to plasma concentration ratio varies by drug: 0.5 for phenytoin, 2 for maprotiline; after death sedimentation, clotting, haemolysis, putrefaction and contamination can make blood results unhelpful and cavity fluids meaningless.

anchors.locator: Quantitative post-mortem analysis › Transfer across barriers, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Single autopsy case: diphenhydramine and dihydrocodeine about tenfold higher in femoral than in heart blood, and tenfold higher again in urine, attributed to diffusion from the bladder; femoral blood can also be altered.

anchors.locator: Quantitative post-mortem analysis › Site-related and time-related differences in post-mortem concentrations, 1st and 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Rouzioux (1980), 10 cases: in 8, left-ventricle post-mortem concentrations 2.58 to 17.66 times those in life; in 2 carbon monoxide deaths about 25-30% lower after death. Mechanisms: redistribution across failing barriers (from gut, organs, bladder, lungs), gain or loss of drug, and chemical change (e.g. hydrolysis raising apparent free morphine).

anchors.locator: Quantitative post-mortem analysis › Relationship between concentrations measured before and after death, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Few human data: post-mortem to ante-mortem ratios for imipramine 4.85, 1.39, 9.94, 7.60 and chloroquine 17.66, 14.6; femoral post-mortem to ante-mortem serum for amitriptyline 3.6, 4.3, 12 and imipramine 3.0, 6.0; single cases from 11.7 (dosulepin) to 1.0 (salicylate), methadone 2.6; MDMA 1.1-6.6 (ref. 68, mismatched); sample timing varied.

anchors.locator: Quantitative post-mortem analysis › Can the extent of post-mortem redistribution be deduced from the properties of a drug?, 1st-2nd paragraphs; Figures 1-2 captions; Table 1
anchors.extracted: Leikin & Watson's approximate central-to-peripheral ratios (Table 1, e.g. morphine 2.2) give no uncertainty, which the author judges very large (fentanyl, 11 cases: 0.89-3.2, mean 1.6). Ratio vs volume of distribution r = 0.247, vs octanol-water partition r = 0.035 (both P > 0.1); ratio exceeds volume of distribution for 15 of 33 drugs.

claims.overstatement: None; the review quotes a single MDMA range, so 'ranges' is better singular; 40-8500 µg/L = 0.04-8.5 mg/L is correct.
claims.note: The review also relays MDMA post-mortem to ante-mortem ratios of 1.1-6.6 (MDA 1.5-13.3), which would give sizes for the claim's statement that MDMA is found higher after death, but the reference given (ref. 68) is a drink-spiking urinalysis paper, so the figures cannot be traced from this source.

anchors.locator: Quantitative post-mortem analysis › Extrapolation from post-mortem concentrations to ante-mortem concentrations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Quoted lethal concentration range for MDMA in modern data 40-8500 µg/L (ref. 38, Gable 2004), given as an example of the difficulty of defining lethal concentrations.

anchors.locator: Quantitative post-mortem analysis › Relationship between concentrations measured before and after death, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Post-mortem to ante-mortem ratios attributed to Elliott: MDMA 1.1-6.6, MDA 1.5-13.3; the cited reference (68) does not match.

anchors.locator: Quantitative post-mortem analysis › Transfer across barriers, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Rabbits given MDMA: heart-blood concentrations rose after death mainly by redistribution from the lungs, and by diffusion from stomach, trachea or oesophagus depending on where the drug was placed (animal data; cadaver studies support the reflux route).
